newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat says Israel about to free female prisoners.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says Israel about to free female prisoners.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Monday Israel would free all its female Palestinian prisoners to Palestinian areas by Wednesday.
Israel announced on Friday it was going to free the 25 women within days, as part of peace agreements with the PLO.
Arafat told Abu Dhabi Television "Tomorrow evening or the day after tomorrow in the morning all the women prisoners will be released."
A PLO official said the female prisoners would be taken to the West Bank town of Ramallah, where Arafat would personally receive them.

Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a summit meeting late on Sunday on the future of the Israeli-PLO peace process, and on Monday the Israeli cabinet met to discuss further troop pullouts from the West Bank,.
The meeting preceded a U.S. visit by Netanyahu later this week, including talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday.

The cabinet meeting centred on presentations by senior military planning and legal officials, who discussed a timetable for future withdrawals, division of military responsibilities, and other issues, the cabinet secretary said in a statement.
"The cabinet will discuss further questions of the redeployment toward the end of the month," he said. Officials said no decisions were taken at the meeting.

An Israel-PLO deal on Hebron set March 7 as the start of a three-stage troop withdrawal from rural areas still under Israeli occupation in the West Bank. The pullbacks are to be completed by mid-1998.

In a breakthrough in January, Israel handed 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to PLO rule, ending months of rancorous debate both with the Palestinians and within Netanyahu's right-wing cabinet.
Arafat arrived in Hebron on Monday to spend the last day of the Moslem feast of Eid al-Fitr in the West Bank.

Foreign Minister David Levy told army radio the cabinet faced a decision on whether the withdrawal would be made in areas currently under joint Israeli-PLO control, or if territory now under exclusive Israeli authority would also be handed over to Palestinian self-rule. Before the Hebron pullout -- agreed with Israel's previous Labour government but suspended after Islamic suicide bombings early last year -- Arabs had voiced fears that the hawkish Netanyahu, elected last May, might bring peace moves to a halt.
Netanyahu said on Sunday he and Arafat had agreed to start detailed talks on future steps outlined in the Hebron pact.
"We agreed on a mechanism to resolve these issues and advance them," he said. Israeli-PLO teams will begin talks next Sunday, after a meeting of an economics panel.

Levy said the cabinet would decide on the additional pullout solely on the basis of security considerations. He reiterated Israel's insistence that it alone would determine the nature and depth of the pullbacks. The PLO insists they must be negotiated.

Arafat has complained of delays on other issues in the Hebron deal, including the operation of Palestinian sea and air ports, the release of Palestinian prisoners and "free passage" between Gaza and the West Bank.

"A month after the Hebron protocol was signed, many things should have been implemented, including the release of women (prisoners), but until now nothing has been implemented," Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdeinah told Reuters on Monday.
U.S. officials have expressed hopes that agreement on Hebron could pave the way for a resumption of talks with Syria.
The Syrian track, seen as the cornerstone to an overall Middle East peace deal, has long been stalled over the strategic Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Netanyahu's office said the prime minister met Golan settlers on Monday to hear their views before his U.S. trip.
